knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Radical Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/problem: The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}$ at the point where $x=1$ is{{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-{x}^{2}+10x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10-2x.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (10-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2(x-5)}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}} \\  & =-\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(-\frac{x-5}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+10x}})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{10-2(1)}{2\sqrt{-(1{)}^{2}+10(1)}} \\  & =\frac{8}{2\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{9+4x}$ at the point where $x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=9+4x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (4) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{9+4x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{2}{\sqrt{9+4x}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{9+4(0)}} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
